# What Parquet is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

Parquet is a file format for tables: named columns, each of one type. Unlike
CSV, it stores a table column by column rather than row by row, and almost
everything that makes it small, fast, or surprising follows from that
(@sec-storage). Working with it comes down to reading and writing files, and to
querying a file or a directory of files without loading them whole
(@sec-usage).

Parquet has no program of its own; libraries read and write it. This document
uses Polars and pandas in Python, the package arrow in R, and DuckDB, which
queries Parquet files with SQL from any of these languages and from the command
line. Most of them build on Apache Arrow, the same columnar layout in memory.

Parquet holds tables. Arrays of more dimensions, such as images or fields on a
grid, belong in [](hdf5.qmd) or [](zarr.qmd).

Checked against pyarrow 26.0, pandas 3.0, Polars 2.0, DuckDB 1.5, and arrow
25.0 for R.


# How Parquet stores a table {#sec-storage}

A CSV file stores a table row by row: every value of the first row, then every
value of the second. Parquet stores it column by column. A file is cut into row
groups, slices of typically a hundred thousand to a million rows, and within a
row group the values of each column lie together, in a column chunk that is
compressed on its own. A footer at the end of the file holds the schema, the
position of every chunk, and statistics of each: its minimum, its maximum, and
its number of nulls. A reader reads the footer first, and then only the chunks
it needs.

The values of one column are alike, so they compress well. A value that
repeats, such as the name of a site, is stored once and referred to by a small
number; a run of equal values is stored as the value and its length; and a
general compression follows, Snappy in pandas and zstd in Polars. A Parquet file
is typically several times smaller than the same table as CSV, and much faster
to read, because nothing is parsed from text.


## Read only what you need {#sec-columns}

The cost of reading a Parquet file grows with the columns read, not with the
columns in the file: reading 3 of 200 columns reads only their chunks. A reader
skips whole row groups too, when their statistics show that no row can match a
filter: a query for one week skips every row group whose times all lie outside
it. The statistics help only where the values of a column are clustered, so
sort a table by the column that queries filter on, such as time or site, before
writing it.

The other side is that reading one row touches a chunk of every column, and
each chunk has to be decompressed. Parquet suits reading many rows of a few
columns, as an analysis does, not looking up single records, as a database
does.


## The types travel with the data {#sec-types}

The schema gives every column its type, so a reader gets back what was
written: integers stay integers, a station code such as `007` stays a string
with its leading zeros, a float keeps every bit, and a timestamp keeps its
precision and whether it refers to UTC. Every column, of any type, can hold
nulls, and in a column of floats a null is not NaN: the two stay apart. Parquet
so avoids most of what text formats lose
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-hand-off)), although a library may still
change the types when it reads a file, as pandas does (@sec-read-write).

Parquet does not store meaning. It has no type for a physical unit: put the
unit into the name of the column, such as `depth_m`, or into the metadata,
pairs of keys and values that a file and each of its columns may carry. pyarrow
keeps the metadata, but a round trip through pandas or Polars drops it, so a
unit that only the metadata holds is easily lost.


## Write once, never edit {#sec-write-once}

A Parquet file cannot be changed in place: no value changed, no row appended,
no column added. The chunks are compressed and the footer that locates them
comes last, so every change rewrites the file. Data that grows, such as
measurements that arrive every day, goes into new files, which a dataset joins
into one table (@sec-datasets).

Because the footer comes last, a file whose writing was interrupted has none,
and every reader fails on it instead of reading half a table as a valid one
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)).


## Datasets: many files, one table {#sec-datasets}

A dataset is a directory of Parquet files with the same columns, which the
readers treat as one table. It is usually partitioned: its files lie in
directories named after the values of a column, such as
`measurements/site=north/`, and the readers take the column from the path. A
query that filters on that column skips whole directories. Partition by a
column with few values that queries filter on, such as site or year. Thousands
of small files are slower to read than a few large ones, because each file has
a footer of its own to read.

A path is text, so the readers guess the type of a partition column from it.
pandas, pyarrow, and Polars take a directory `station=007` for the integer 7,
which loses the leading zeros and no longer matches the station `007` in other
tables ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-no-guess)); DuckDB keeps it as a
string. Give the type when reading, such as
`hive_schema={"station": pl.String}` in Polars, or partition only by columns
whose values cannot be mistaken. Do not rely on the order of the rows across
the files of a dataset; sort when order matters.


# Working with Parquet {#sec-usage}

The libraries do the same few things under different names. Each one reads a
single file and a dataset alike.


## Read and write a file {#sec-read-write}

```python
import pandas as pd
import polars as pl

samples = pl.read_parquet("samples.parquet", columns=["sample_id", "depth_m"])
samples.write_parquet("depths.parquet")

samples = pd.read_parquet("samples.parquet", columns=["sample_id", "depth_m"],
                          dtype_backend="pyarrow")
samples.to_parquet("depths.parquet", index=False)
```

```r
library(arrow)

samples <- read_parquet("samples.parquet", col_select = c(sample_id, depth_m))
write_parquet(samples, "depths.parquet")
```

Name the columns to read (@sec-columns). pandas, with its default types from
NumPy, reads an integer column with nulls as floats and both nulls and NaN as
NaN, so a round trip through pandas changes the file: the integers come back as
floats, and the NaN as nulls. `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` keeps the types of the
file. `index=False` keeps the index of pandas out of the file; otherwise, after
a filter for example, other libraries read it as an extra column,
`__index_level_0__`. pandas compresses with Snappy unless told otherwise;
`compression="zstd"` gives smaller files.


## Query without loading {#sec-query}

```python
measurements = (
    pl.scan_parquet("measurements/")
    .filter(pl.col("site") == "north")
    .select("time", "temperature_c")
    .collect()
)
```

```r
library(dplyr)

measurements <- open_dataset("measurements/") |>
  filter(site == "north") |>
  select(time, temperature_c) |>
  collect()
```

```sql
SELECT time, temperature_c
FROM 'measurements/*/*.parquet'
WHERE site = 'north';
```

A lazy query, `scan_parquet` in Polars, `open_dataset` in R, or SQL in DuckDB,
reads only the columns and the row groups that its selection and its filter
need (@sec-columns), so it handles even a table larger than memory, as long as
the result fits. In pandas, `read_parquet` takes `columns` and `filters`, such
as `filters=[("site", "==", "north")]`. DuckDB runs the same SQL on the command
line, as `duckdb -c "SELECT …"`.


## Write a dataset {#sec-write-dataset}

| Library | Writes a dataset partitioned by `site` |
|----------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Polars | `df.write_parquet("measurements/", partition_by="site")` |
| pandas | `df.to_parquet("measurements/", partition_cols=["site"])` |
| R arrow | `write_dataset(df, "measurements/", partitioning = "site")` |
| DuckDB | `COPY t TO 'measurements' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (site))` |

To add data to a dataset, write a new file into the directory of its partition,
such as one file a month into `measurements/site=north/` (@sec-write-once).


## Look inside a file {#sec-inspect}

```bash
duckdb -c "DESCRIBE 'samples.parquet'"                  # its columns, types
duckdb -c "FROM parquet_metadata('samples.parquet')"    # its row groups
duckdb -c "FROM parquet_kv_metadata('samples.parquet')" # its metadata
```

A Parquet file describes itself: the footer gives its columns, their types, the
row groups, and their statistics, without reading the data. In Python,
`pyarrow.parquet.read_schema` shows the columns, the types, and the metadata,
and `read_metadata` the row groups. A step that reads a file can so check it
against the schema it expects
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-hand-off)).
